main_damage_causes: Ginny's emotional expressiveness and personality are collapsed into a single functional line, erasing her as a characterized presence in her debut scene.
Her recognizing and reacting to Harry — a relationship-seeding beat explicit in the book corpus — is entirely absent from the film corpus.
The physically and emotionally vivid moment of her running after the train (half-laughing, half-crying) is dropped, removing the scene's most humanizing characterization of her.

Removal of Ginny's active resistance arc — specifically the attempted breakfast confession (book Scenes 91-105) — which is the primary evidence that she is not a passive victim but a character fighting against possession, gutting her agency and interiority entirely

Compression and trivialisation of her psychological deterioration under possession into isolated background details and a single comedic aside, preventing the audience from developing sustained concern or understanding of her internal struggle

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 — Platform 9¾, Ginny's only line is 'Good luck'
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book corpus, Ginny is an eager, emotionally expressive child: she begs to go on the train to see Harry, cries when her brothers leave, runs alongside the train waving, and is shown pointing and squealing 'Harry Potter!' at King's Cross the following year. She is animated, funny, and emotionally present.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Ginny's entire contribution at Platform 9¾ is reduced to a single two-word line — 'Good luck.' — directed at Harry. She has no other dialogue, no visible emotional reaction to her brothers leaving, and no characterization beyond being a silent bystander.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book establishes Ginny as lively, emotionally demonstrative, and already infatuated with Harry in an endearing, childlike way. The film reduces her to a functional extra with a single polite line, stripping her of the personality that makes her memorable and sets up her character arc.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 — Ginny's reaction to brothers departing is absent
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book corpus explicitly describes Ginny crying when her brothers board the train, then running alongside it laughing and crying simultaneously until it outpaces her — a vivid, emotionally textured moment that establishes her bond with her brothers and her big feelings.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: No such moment occurs in the film corpus. Ginny is shown at the wall and delivers 'Good luck,' but there is no depiction of her emotional response to her brothers leaving or any attempt to keep up with the train.
damaging_scenes.explanation: A small but characterizing beat is lost. The half-laughing, half-crying run after the train is the most humanizing moment Ginny gets in the book's opening — it shows her warmth and her closeness to her brothers. Its absence leaves her as a cipher rather than a person.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 — Ginny's Harry Potter recognition/excitement absent
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book corpus (Scenes 4–8, 13–15) shows Ginny recognizing Harry at King's Cross, squealing 'Harry Potter!', pointing at him, begging to go on the train to see him, and being gently scolded. This establishes her awareness of Harry, her excitability, and seeds her eventual romantic arc in an organic, age-appropriate way.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In the film corpus, Ginny has no such reaction to Harry. She does not recognize him, squeal, point, or express any excitement about his presence. The entire beat of Ginny noticing Harry is absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is a foundational beat for the Ginny–Harry relationship. Her starstruck, then genuine, fascination with Harry is the first layer of what becomes a central romance in the saga. Removing it means their eventual relationship has less grounded, earned setup from the very first film. The corpus supports this as a clear divergence with relationship-level consequences.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 - The Burrow kitchen, Ginny's first appearance
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 2-5 establish that Ginny gives a small squeal and runs out, and Ron explains she 'never shuts up normally' — her shyness around Harry is a temporary, crush-based anomaly against a baseline of being talkative and confident.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Ginny squeals and dashes back up the stairs. Ron's line is condensed to 'Been talking about you all summer. Dead annoying, really.' The book's specific contrast — that her silence is weird because she normally never shuts up — is lost. The film presents her shyness without the counterweight of her usual confident personality.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book carefully frames Ginny's shyness as an exception to her normally outspoken character, which seeds her as a person of substance. The film omits Ron's clarifying line ('she never shuts up normally'), leaving audiences with only the shy, star-struck impression — the beginning of a pattern that reduces her to a one-note crush.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 - Flourish and Blotts, Ginny defends Harry against Draco
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 31 establishes this as the first time Ginny speaks in front of Harry — a moment of real courage and agency where she glares at Malfoy and says 'Leave him alone, he didn't want all that!' The book narrator notes it is the first time she has spoken in front of Harry, marking it as a significant character beat.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film includes Ginny's line ('Leave him alone! He didn't want all that!') and it is present in the corpus. However, the film does not mark the moment as her first speech in front of Harry, and the narrative weight of the moment — that this shy girl found her voice to defend someone — is not signalled to the audience.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book explicitly flags this as her first words in Harry's presence, making it a quiet but meaningful assertion of her character beneath the shyness. The film delivers the line but strips the context that makes it resonate as a character-defining moment of bravery breaking through embarrassment.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 3 - Library/Dueling Club aftermath, Ginny scribbling in diary
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 91-101 establish Ginny as increasingly disturbed and trying to confess something important — she is visibly tense, rocking like Dobby, and nearly tells Harry something crucial about the Chamber before Percy interrupts. Her internal torment is active and externally readable.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film (Scene 3, library sequence) shows Ginny 'tired and pale, scribbles furiously in a small black book' — but this is presented as atmospheric background detail. Her active attempt to confess and her clear psychological distress are absent from the film corpus. The audience sees her writing in the diary passively, not struggling against Riddle's control.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book gives Ginny active interiority — she is fighting to warn Harry, barely holding herself together. The film reduces her to a pale background figure scribbling, which strips her of the dramatic tension of her internal struggle and makes her victimhood appear passive rather than a genuine battle against possession.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 3 - Dueling Club, Ginny bolts the room after Parseltongue incident
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 75-78 show Ginny as genuinely frightened and disturbed by events related to the Chamber, with context that she is being controlled by the diary. Book Scene 84 shows her staring in terror from the diary to Harry when Malfoy finds it — she is afraid Harry will discover what she has done.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 3 (Dueling Club): 'Ginny bolts the room' after Harry speaks Parseltongue. Later in the corridor scene (Film Scene 4), Ginny stares at the diary in Harry's hands 'with utter terror on her face' then dashes off. These are present in the corpus but function only as spooky atmosphere — the film never gives Ginny any lines or interiority to explain her terror to the audience.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The film uses Ginny's fear as visual shorthand for 'something is wrong' without ever giving the audience access to why she is so afraid. Without the attempted confession scene (book Scenes 91-105), her panicked reactions read as inexplicable rather than as the agonised behaviour of a possessed girl trying to warn people while being prevented.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 4 - Corridor, Harry finds the diary, Ginny's reaction
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 84 establishes that Ginny recognises the diary immediately and is terrified Harry will discover her secrets from it. This directly connects to her earlier attempted confession and her internal war.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 4: Ginny stands at the end of the corridor, 'looking from the diary to Harry — utter terror on her face — then dashes off.' Harry calls after her: 'Ginny! I was only joking.' Ron says 'Brilliant. Even your sister thinks I'm the monster now.' The film plays Ginny's terror as a misunderstanding about Harry's joke, flattening her meaningful panic into comic relief about Harry's reputation.
damaging_scenes.explanation: In the book, Ginny's terror at seeing the diary is deeply meaningful — it is about her own guilt and fear of exposure. The film recontextualises it as just another person being afraid of Harry-the-suspected-heir, destroying the specific, character-driven significance of her reaction and reducing her to a prop in a joke at Harry and Ron's expense.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 4 - Absent scene: Ginny's attempted breakfast confession (book Scenes 91-105)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 91-105 are a sustained, important sequence: Ginny sits down with Ron and Harry, visibly tense and rocking, and is clearly on the verge of confessing to them about the Chamber. She is interrupted by Percy. This is one of the most important windows into her active agency and her fight against Riddle's control. It also sets up why Dumbledore later says 'she tried to tell you' — Ginny was not a passive victim.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: This scene does not appear anywhere in the film corpus. There is no moment where Ginny attempts to confess or warn Harry. Her entire arc of internal resistance to Riddle's control is absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The attempted confession is the single most important demonstration that Ginny is not merely a passive victim of possession — she fights it, she tries to protect Harry and expose the truth at personal risk. Its absence means the film Ginny has no visible agency in her own story. The audience never sees her struggling against Riddle, which fundamentally damages her as a character and makes her possession seem like helpless victimhood rather than a battle she partially fought.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 4 - Quidditch staircase, Ron notices Ginny is acting oddly
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book builds a pattern of Ginny's visible deterioration — pale, distraught, emotionally volatile — which the reader understands as possession. Ron's observation in the film corpus ('she gets weirder and weirder by the day') is present but isolated.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 4 (staircase): Ron says 'Hey, Ginny! Going to the match?' and Ginny 'looks up, startled, then shakes her head and exits.' Ron says 'I tell you, she gets weirder and weirder by the day.' This is the film's primary characterisation of Ginny's deterioration — a single throwaway line played for mild comedy.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book develops Ginny's deterioration across multiple scenes with emotional specificity. The film compresses her entire psychological unravelling under possession into one comedic aside from Ron. This trivialises what should be a horrifying, sympathetic arc and robs Ginny of the audience's sustained concern for her.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 4 - Chamber of Secrets, Ginny's awakening and confession
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 169-171: Ginny wakes, takes in the scene, and gives a detailed, emotionally rich confession — 'I tried to tell you at b-breakfast,' referencing her specific failed attempt, showing she actively tried to resist and warn Harry. She weeps about being expelled, about having looked forward to Hogwarts since Bill attended. Her first concern after survival is her family's reaction and her future.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 4 (Chamber): Ginny says 'Harry. It was me! But I swear, I didn't mean to... Riddle made me. He wrote to me... took me over... I didn't even know whose diary it was. I found it inside my cauldron.' There is no reference to trying to tell Harry at breakfast. Her confession is shorter and removes the specific evidence of her active resistance. She then immediately notices 'Harry. You're hurt...' and shifts focus to him.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The reference to trying to warn Harry at breakfast is the payoff to a character arc of active resistance that has been entirely cut from the film. Without that line, Ginny's awakening confession is a passive account of victimhood rather than a demonstration that she fought back. The film version also pivots her attention to Harry's wound almost immediately, further centring him over her own traumatic experience.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 4 - Dumbledore's office, Ginny's exoneration scene
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 198-211: Harry agonises about whether to mention Ginny and the diary, worrying about her expulsion. Ginny sobs her explanation to her parents and Dumbledore directly ('His d-diary! I've b-been writing in it...'). Mr. Weasley's response ('Haven't I taught you anything...') and Dumbledore's gentle comfort are all directed at Ginny present in the room. The scene is centred on Ginny's exoneration.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 4 (Dumbledore's office): Ginny is present and speaks ('I didn't know whose diary it was, sir. I swear...'), but her emotional breakdown and her parents' specific responses are partially offscreen — Mrs. Weasley's 'A diary that writes back to you! Honestly, Ginny!' is heard as Ginny is led out by McGonagall, rather than a full in-room confrontation. Mr. Weasley's direct admonishment of Ginny is absent from the film corpus.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's exoneration scene is important for the Weasley family dynamic — Arthur's loving but firm parental response, and Dumbledore's kind reassurance directly to Ginny's face, establish her relationship with her family and her recovery. The film moves key emotional beats offscreen, weakening the relational resolution of her arc.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 4 - Absent scene: Train compartment ending, Ginny reveals Percy's secret (book Scenes 220-225)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 220-225: On the Hogwarts Express, Ginny is 'perfectly happy again' and joins Harry, Ron, Fred, George, and Hermione in a compartment. She giggles and reveals Percy's secret girlfriend, showing she has recovered, is socially integrated with the group, and has her own wit and knowledge. This is the last image of Ginny in CoS — confident, funny, part of the gang.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: This scene does not appear in the film corpus. Ginny has no closing scene that demonstrates her recovery, reintegration, or personality. Her arc ends at the Chamber/Dumbledore's office with trauma and relief but no restoration of her as a full person.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's closing Ginny scene is structurally important: it confirms her recovery and reveals her as witty, socially perceptive, and at ease — the person Ron said she normally is. Without it, the film leaves Ginny defined entirely by her victimisation. The audience never sees who she actually is beyond the traumatised first-year, which damages both her arc and the foundation for her later importance in the series.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 (Leaky Cauldron) — Ginny's arrival with family
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 5 establishes that Ginny, though embarrassed around Harry, is a present and emotionally textured character: she goes red, mutters hello, and her crush-based embarrassment is a defined personality beat. Book Scene 8 shows her giggling at Fred and George's irreverence, and Scene 22 shows her sharing a conspiratorial laugh with Harry over Percy's pomposity — establishing a nascent, genuine rapport.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In Film Scene 1, Ginny's arrival is entirely absorbed into the family ensemble chaos. She has no individual moment, no reaction to Harry, no embarrassment, no personality beat. She is visually present but functionally invisible.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book uses this early Leaky Cauldron gathering to plant seeds of Ginny's personality and her specific dynamic with Harry. The film collapses her into background noise, removing the relational groundwork that the saga depends on for her later centrality to Harry's arc.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 (Leaky Cauldron continuation) — Ginny's one line about Fred's nose
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 22 shows Ginny sharing a private laugh with Harry — a small but meaningful moment of genuine connection and mutual wit. Book Scene 5 establishes her embarrassed awareness of Harry as emotionally significant. Her personality in the books is warm, observant, and capable of dry humor.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Ginny's sole contribution in Film Scene 2 is correcting Fred about whose nose appears larger in the photograph ('That's your nose, Fred'). This is a throwaway comedic line with no emotional weight or connection to Harry. It functions purely as a setup for Fred's joke, not as characterization.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Ginny is reduced to a straight-man prop for a sibling joke. Her one spoken moment in the film corpus has no individuality and no relational dimension. The book's version of this gathering gives her specific, textured reactions; the film gives her a single functional line that could belong to any sibling.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 3 (Gryffindor corridor) — Ginny reports the Fat Lady's portrait
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 33 shows Ginny as emotionally vulnerable but present after the Dementor encounter — shaking, needing comfort, but part of the group. Book Scene 25 shows her reacting with indignation ('Oh, that's nice') when dismissed by Ron, demonstrating she pushes back rather than simply absorbing mistreatment. She is a participant, not a messenger.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In Film Scene 3, Ginny appears with an 'ashen' face to deliver the plot-critical news about the Fat Lady's destroyed portrait. Ron dismisses her report ('Probably stuffing her face with apples again') and she corrects him ('No. You don't understand —'), but the scene immediately pivots away from her to Hermione's reaction and Dumbledore's arrival. Ginny functions here purely as an exposition delivery mechanism.
damaging_scenes.explanation: While Ginny does speak and is briefly present, she exists solely to transmit plot information before being sidelined. Her emotional state ('ashen') is noted but not developed. The dismissal by Ron is not given the interpersonal texture the books provide. She is a narrative tool rather than a character participant. This is not catastrophic in isolation but is consistent with a pattern of functional reduction.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 – Death Eater attack at the campsite
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 64: Fred grabs Ginny's hand and pulls her toward the wood, establishing her as someone being physically guided to safety by her brother. Book Scene 73 shows Fred, George, and Ginny returning unhurt but shaken, indicating they navigated the chaos together. Ginny is present and part of the group action.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Arthur assigns Ginny explicitly as a responsibility to Fred and George: 'Fred, George! Ginny is your responsibility. Go!' Ginny has no lines, no reactions, and no individual presence during the attack sequence. She is reduced to a passive charge to be protected rather than a participant.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The film frames Ginny purely as someone to be shepherded, stripping her of any individual agency or reaction during a major dramatic sequence. The book similarly has Fred guide her but does not reduce her to a named dependency in Arthur's orders. It is a small but telling signal of how the film treats her as peripheral.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 – Portkey journey and arrival at campsite
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 2–3 establish Ginny as a present, smiling, self-aware young girl. Book Scenes 10, 13, 17 show her contributing observations and opinions naturally in group conversation. Book Scene 47 shows her making an astute observation about Bagman's security lapse, demonstrating she is engaged and perceptive.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Ginny's only contribution in the entire extended campsite arrival and World Cup sequence is a single exclamation: 'Look!' She has no lines of substance, no named reactions at the Portkey, and no perceptible individual characterization. Arthur's repeated 'Keep up, girls!' bundles her anonymously with Hermione.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book uses the World Cup journey to establish Ginny as observant, funny, and engaged. The film gives her one word and folds her into background scenery. Her perceptive comment about Bagman (book Scene 47) is entirely absent, and she has no conversational presence across a lengthy sequence, resulting in a flat, undifferentiated background character.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 4 – Yule Ball invitation subplot (Ron comforted by Ginny after Fleur rejection)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 92 shows Ginny comforting Ron after his Fleur humiliation while also 'fighting back a smile' – she is simultaneously sympathetic and amused, showing emotional complexity. Book Scene 98–108 shows Ginny pushing back ('Don't laugh'), defending Hermione's secret, refusing Ron's presumptuous offer to take her to the ball, and then going scarlet with her own embarrassment about Neville. She asserts herself, keeps confidences, and shows wounded pride.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 4: Ginny comforts Ron with 'It's all right, Ron. It's okay, Ron. It's all right. It doesn't matter.' She then volunteers the information about Fleur to Harry and Hermione, and when asked what Ron did, she adds the comic detail 'Actually, he sort of screamed at her. It was a bit frightening.' She has no scene equivalent to her refusal of Ron's presumptuous offer, no defense of Hermione's secret, and no moment of her own wounded pride about going with Neville.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The film reduces Ginny's role in this subplot to a supportive bystander and comic narrator. The book's version gives her assertiveness (refusing to be assigned as Ron's date), loyalty (refusing to reveal Hermione's secret), and vulnerability (going scarlet about Neville). All of this is absent. What remains is a purely functional scene-explainer role with no personal stakes.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 4 – Dress robes reveal ('I'm not wearing that, it's ghastly')
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 81–82 is a brief exchange where Ron mistakes Ginny's dress for his own. Ginny is not given a separate line about the robes; the joke is about Ron's humiliation. Book Scene 30 shows Ginny confidently defending Bill's long hair against Mrs. Weasley's old-fashioned taste, showing she has her own aesthetic opinions.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 4: Ron says 'Ginny, these must be for you' and Ginny replies 'I'm not wearing that, it's ghastly.' This is a small added moment.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is a minor addition that is broadly consistent with Ginny's book personality (she has opinions on style, per book Scene 30), so damage is minimal. It is noted for completeness but does not meaningfully misrepresent her. Impact is low.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 5 – Yule Ball dancing (Ginny and Neville background appearance)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 109 establishes Ginny dancing with Neville nearby Harry, with Ginny wincing as Neville treads on her feet. She is present but this is a brief background note. The book has already established her emotional investment in Harry and the awkwardness of going with Neville (Scene 108).
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 5 and 6: Ginny and Neville appear briefly in background shots dancing. No emotional context is given for why she is there with Neville, what she feels about Harry, or any trace of the wounded pride and resigned disappointment the book establishes in Scene 108. Film Scene 6 shows Neville dancing with Ginny in the Great Hall while Hermione cries on the staircase, again as pure background.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The film never establishes that Ginny wanted to go with Harry, that she accepted Neville only because she had no other option, or that her ball experience carries any emotional weight for her. Her entire arc around the ball – from scarlet embarrassment in Scene 108 to resigned misery – is invisible. Given that this period is foundational for the slow-burn Harry/Ginny relationship, the absence is a meaningful loss of relationship groundwork.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 7 – Second task preparation (Fred and George's betting scene)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 112–113 show Ginny sitting with Fred, George, Harry, and others at lunch, having a good time together – establishing her as a natural, comfortable presence in Harry's social world during a tense period.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 7: Fred and George are shown taking bets in front of the crowd before the second task. Ginny appears only to briefly say 'Don't be so mean' to Fred and George about their callous betting odds. This is her only line in the second task sequence.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The line is consistent with her character (she has a conscience and pushes back on her brothers), but it is an isolated reaction with no follow-through. The broader loss is that her comfortable social integration into Harry's world during this period is invisible. Damage is minor.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 – Grimmauld Place arrival/kitchen scene
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book establishes Ginny as an active, resourceful presence at Grimmauld Place: she investigates the Imperturbable Charm on the kitchen door using Dungbombs, reports her findings to Fred and George, reacts with fierce indignation ('noise like an angry cat') to Percy's insults about the family, participates in the Order dinner conversation, interjects with opinions (e.g., 'Bill doesn't like him either'), and rages loudly at being sent to bed – enough to set off Mrs. Black's portrait.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In the film Ginny's only line at Grimmauld Place is a brief 'Hi, Mum!' She is present as a background figure but has no investigative action, no verbal sparring, no emotional reaction to Percy, and no defiant protest at being excluded. Her entire characterisation at headquarters is reduced to a single greeting.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book uses the Grimmauld Place sequence to establish Ginny as clever, opinionated, emotionally invested in her family, and willing to push back against authority. Stripping all of this to a single line removes the first sustained look at who book-Ginny is, leaving the film audience with no foundation for her personality.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 – DA formation meeting at the Hog's Head
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book Ginny contributes substantively to the Hog's Head meeting: she is one of the voices who confirms Harry's credentials ('It's true'), and later it is established that she recruited Michael Corner and his Ravenclaw friends by telling Michael about the meeting, directly enabling the DA's formation. She also proposes naming the group 'Dumbledore's Army' ('Yeah, the DA's good… let's make it stand for Dumbledore's Army, because that's the Ministry's worst fear, isn't it?').
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In the film Ginny speaks one confirmatory line ('It's true') at the pub meeting. The naming of the group ('Dumbledore's Army') is not attributed to her in the film corpus – there is no scene in the provided film text where she proposes the name. Her role in recruiting Michael Corner and his group is entirely absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Ginny's twin contributions – recruiting a significant portion of the DA and coining the group's defining name – are either absent or transferred away. The name 'Dumbledore's Army' becomes one of the saga's iconic phrases; removing Ginny's authorship of it is a concrete loss of agency and narrative credit.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 – DA training sessions in the Room of Requirement
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book describes Ginny performing well in DA sessions – notably she is doing 'very well' with jinxes, better than her partner Michael Corner. She is also described casting spells competently throughout. Her flying/Quidditch skill is discussed by Fred and George as evidence of her hidden talent ('Come on, Ginny's not bad'). This competence is built up across multiple scenes.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In the film Ginny casts 'Reducto!' once during the DA session and is briefly shown. Harry singles her out with 'Fantastic, Ginny!' but this is a fleeting moment with no context. The extended portrait of her as a notably skilled student within the DA is absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Minor loss: the moment is present but thin. The book's cumulative establishment of Ginny's competence across DA sessions is compressed to a single exclamation, which is too brief to build the audience's perception of her as genuinely gifted.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 3 – Umbridge's office / plan to contact Sirius
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book it is Ginny who devises the cover story for keeping students away from Umbridge's corridor ('Garrotting Gas'), delivers it convincingly with improvised logic ('we'll have your body as proof'), and volunteers immediately to help despite not knowing the full plan. She also participates actively in the plan alongside Luna. The book explicitly notes Hermione's surprise at 'the readiness with which Ginny had come up with this lie.'
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In the film the scene at Umbridge's office corridor is not depicted with Ginny in a speaking, active role for this portion of the plan. The Garrotting Gas cover story is absent from the film corpus. Ginny appears later outside Umbridge's office having escaped using 'Puking Pastilles' but the corridor guard scene with its demonstration of her quick thinking is not shown.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The Garrotting Gas scene is one of the clearest demonstrations of Ginny's independent quick-wittedness and composure under pressure. Its absence removes a moment specifically noted in the book as surprising even Hermione, which would have landed as a character-defining beat for the film audience.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 3 – Ginny's argument to join the Ministry rescue
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book Ginny makes a forceful, reasoned argument for her right to join the mission: 'I'm three years older than you were when you fought You-Know-Who over the Philosopher's Stone, and it's because of me that Malfoy's stuck back in Umbridge's office with giant flying bogies attacking him.' She rejects Harry's paternalism directly and her jaw-set expression is compared to Fred and George, showing family steel. The book also notes she performed the Bat-Bogey Hex on Malfoy to enable the escape – explicitly credited by Ron.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In the film Ginny's participation in the group joining Harry is shown but her specific argument and the explicit credit for the Bat-Bogey Hex are absent from the film corpus. She says 'Puking Pastilles, it wasn't pretty' but the forceful defence of her right to come and the specific Bat-Bogey credit ('Ginny was best, she got Malfoy') are not present.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is one of Ginny's most assertive moments in the entire book, directly pushing back against Harry's underestimation of her. It also gives her concrete credit for the action that enabled the group's escape. Both the argument and the explicit heroic credit are lost, flattening her into a passive participant in the group rather than someone who earned her place and proved her value.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 3 – Department of Mysteries battle
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book Ginny sustains a broken ankle during the battle – she is immobilised but continues to attempt action (screaming warning about Ron and the brain, contributing awareness of the threat). She is Stunned by a Death Eater while immobilised. Luna supports her and helps her move despite the injury. Her injury is treated as a real cost: she cannot walk and has to be supported. In the hospital wing aftermath she participates actively in conversation.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In the film corpus Ginny casts 'Reducto!' during the battle and is present throughout, but there is no depiction of her receiving a broken ankle or being incapacitated. The injury arc – which both costs her and shows her continuing to fight through it – is absent from the film corpus shown.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The broken ankle matters because it shows Ginny suffering real consequences and still trying to act, and it makes the battle feel costly for the whole group. Its absence slightly sanitises her participation and removes one of the few moments where her vulnerability and determination are shown simultaneously.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 – Ginny's possession backstory and Harry's crisis (Christmas at Grimmauld Place)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book Ginny proactively seeks out Harry when he is isolating himself over fear of possession, confronts him directly ('that was a bit stupid of you'), and draws on her own experience of Voldemort's possession in Chamber of Secrets to give him concrete, authoritative reassurance. The exchange ('Lucky you' / 'I'm sorry') shows her emotional complexity: residual pain about her own possession, sharpness with Harry for ignoring her, and genuine compassion. This is the only scene where someone with direct experience validates Harry.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: This scene – Ginny approaching Harry in the bedroom with Ron and Hermione, her confronting him about hiding, and the possession diagnostic exchange – does not appear in the film corpus. The film shows Harry at Grimmauld Place at Christmas and his possession fears are addressed via Snape/Occlumency and Sirius, but Ginny's unique, personal contribution to resolving Harry's crisis is entirely absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is arguably the most important scene for Ginny's individual relationship with Harry. It is the only moment in the saga where she draws on her Chamber of Secrets trauma to meaningfully help him, establishes her as someone with unique authority on this specific subject, and creates a genuine emotional bond between them outside the wider group. Its complete removal is a major structural loss: it eliminates the foundation for their eventual romantic relationship and removes Ginny's most significant independent agency in the entire book.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 – Library scene / Easter egg / Sirius plan
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book Ginny seeks Harry out in the library, brings him an Easter egg from Mrs Weasley, notices his emotional state, engages him in genuine one-on-one conversation, and – crucially – is the one who proposes and enables the plan to contact Sirius through the fire in Umbridge's office: 'Well, if you really want to talk to Sirius, I expect we could think of a way to do it.' She then goes to Fred and George to set it up. The scene ends with them being chased out of the library together.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The library scene is entirely absent from the film corpus. The plan to contact Sirius via Umbridge's fireplace originates differently in the film, with no scene showing Ginny as the initiator or the intimate one-on-one conversation with Harry that precedes it.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This scene gives Ginny two things the film removes: (1) the agency of originating the plan that drives the plot toward the Ministry, and (2) a private, warm moment with Harry that builds their relationship organically. Without it, Ginny's connection to Harry is purely group-based and her role in the plot's mechanics disappears. This is a substantial double loss of agency and relationship development.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 – Ron/Ginny dating subplot (Michael Corner revelation)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book includes a developed subplot in which Ginny is secretly dating Michael Corner (having given up on Harry), Ron reacts with outrage, and Hermione explains that Ginny moved on. This establishes Ginny as someone with an active romantic and social life, independent of Harry, and demonstrates she has agency over her own feelings. By the end of OotP she has also dumped Michael for being sulky after a Quidditch loss and mentions Dean Thomas as her next choice – showing her confidence and self-direction.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The Michael Corner subplot, Ron's reaction to it, and Ginny's own romantic independence are entirely absent from the film corpus. There is no scene establishing that Ginny has moved on from Harry or that she has her own dating life. Her romantic trajectory is invisible.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This subplot is essential for the eventual Harry/Ginny relationship to feel earned rather than sudden. It establishes Ginny as a person with her own desires, confidence, and social life – not simply waiting for Harry. Removing it means the film audience has no sense of Ginny as a romantic agent, which damages both her character perception and the groundwork for their later relationship.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 – Quidditch subplot (Ginny as Seeker, Ginny's skill acknowledged)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book devotes considerable space to Ginny stepping up as Seeker when Harry is banned, performing creditably (catching the Snitch against Hufflepuff despite difficult conditions), and being discussed by Fred, George and Harry as a genuinely talented player who developed her skills in secret. This is part of a sustained portrait of her as competent and impressive in her own right.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The Quidditch subplot involving Ginny as Seeker, her catch, and the discussions about her hidden talent are entirely absent from the film corpus. The film's Quidditch content does not include this material.
damaging_scenes.explanation: While Quidditch subplots are reasonably compressible, this material specifically builds Ginny's independent competence and self-reliance. Its absence contributes to the film's overall failure to establish her as impressive in her own right, which compounds across all other absences.

damaging_scenes.scene: HBP Film Corpus Scene 1-4 (Burrow arrival / Ginny discovers Harry)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Ginny's first appearance in HBP is as a confident, slightly irritable presence who 'slouches' in and sits on Harry's bed, complaining about Fleur with sharp wit and sarcasm. She is self-possessed and socially at ease from the start.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film invents an entirely new scene where Ginny discovers Harry's trunk and owl and runs around the house asking about him, playing a comedic 'where is he?' routine. She is rendered as excitable and mildly flustered by Harry's presence, with a 'great grinning hug' described as 'oddly charged' and 'a surprise to both of them.' This telegraphs romantic feeling immediately rather than letting it develop organically through Ginny's confidence and independence.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's Ginny is never flustered or girlishly excited about Harry. She treats him as a peer and equal from the first scene. The film immediately frames her through a romantic lens and makes her reactive to Harry rather than self-contained, undermining the book's careful construction of her as someone who has grown past her earlier crush into a confident young woman Harry admires precisely because she doesn't orbit him.

damaging_scenes.scene: HBP Film Corpus Scene 6 (Weasley's Wizard Wheezes - love potion exchange)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Ginny at Weasley's Wizard Wheezes is sharp, funny, and assertive. She raises an eyebrow skeptically at the love potions ('Do they work?'), shuts Fred and George down with a Mrs. Weasley-ish glare when they pry about her boyfriends, and defends herself to Ron with wit and directness. She is entirely in control of the interaction.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film condenses her role. She deflects Fred's question about Dean with 'None of your business' and that is largely the extent of her characterisation in this scene. The Pygmy Puff purchase, the skeptical love potion inquiry, the sharp glare that silences Fred, and the multi-boyfriend teasing that reveals her confident romantic history are all either cut or flattened.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book scene is one of the richest portraits of Ginny's confident, humorous, self-assured personality in the whole novel. The film retains only a token exchange and loses the texture that makes her feel like a fully realised character with her own social world and sharp wit.

damaging_scenes.scene: HBP Film Corpus Scene 7 (Hogwarts Express - Ginny with Dean)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: On the train, Ginny is socially independent and warm. When Harry asks if she wants to find a compartment together, she declines because she has plans with Dean, leaving Harry with 'a strange twinge of annoyance.' She is described moving away with her 'long red hair dancing behind her.' This is the first beat of Harry noticing her as something other than Ron's sister.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film shows Ginny passively sitting in the aisle with Dean, who is whispering to her. She is 'more interested in the Purple Pygmy Puff perched on her shoulder' than in Dean. She interacts briefly with Luna. She is a background figure here rather than the socially active, independently purposeful person she is in the book.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book uses this scene to plant the first seed of Harry's growing awareness of Ginny, specifically triggered by her independent departure. The film does not register this beat at all, weakening the organic build of their relationship.

damaging_scenes.scene: HBP Film Corpus Scene 8 (Great Hall - Ginny dabs Harry's face)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, when Harry arrives at the feast bloodied, Ginny is present at the table but the focus is on Hermione cleaning his face. Ginny's role at this point in the novel is as a peer in a group context, not as someone physically tending to Harry.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film has Ginny pick up a damp napkin and begin to dab Harry's face, then 'feels suddenly awkward' and hands it to him. This small invented moment of physical intimacy followed by awkwardness frames the relationship in a shy, romantically self-conscious register that is not present in the book at this early stage.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The film substitutes the book's slow-burn, self-aware romantic development with early-planted moments of shy physical chemistry. This changes the texture of the relationship from one grounded in mutual respect and growing awareness into a more conventional screen-romance shorthand. Ginny's slight awkwardness here is the opposite of her book characterisation as someone who has deliberately become relaxed and natural around Harry.

damaging_scenes.scene: HBP Film Corpus Scene 10 (Common room - Ginny discovers the Half-Blood Prince inscription)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, it is Ginny who notices Harry's concern about the Prince's book echoing the Tom Riddle diary situation. She speaks to Harry privately and with genuine alarm: 'Did I hear right? You've been taking orders from something someone wrote in a book, Harry?' Her response is driven by lived trauma - she was possessed through Riddle's diary - and Harry has to reassure her. This is a meaningful character moment connecting her past to the present plot.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film has Ginny simply pluck the book from Harry's hand and read the inscription aloud ('Who's the Half-Blood Prince?') in a casual, curious register. There is no alarm, no personal resonance with the diary, no private exchange with Harry about it. She just reads the cover and prompts the others' curiosity.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is a significant loss. In the book, Ginny's reaction to the Prince's book is one of the clearest demonstrations of her depth as a character - she connects the danger Harry might be in to her own traumatic experience, showing intelligence, courage, and hard-won wisdom. The film reduces her to a narrative device who simply names the mystery, stripping her of the very characterisation that makes her more than a love interest.

damaging_scenes.scene: HBP Film Corpus Scene 13 (Slughorn's supper - Ginny arrives flustered with red eyes)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Ginny ends up at Slughorn's lunch because she hexed Zacharias Smith for pestering her about the Ministry battle, and Slughorn was so impressed by her Bat-Bogey Hex that he invited her. She is the only guest there on her own merit rather than family connections. She is composed and staunch - she backs Harry up against Zabini and defends Neville. Slughorn notes she performed 'the most marvelous Bat-Bogey Hex.'
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film has Ginny arrive late to Slughorn's supper with red eyes, 'uncharacteristically flustered,' because she and Dean have been fighting. Hermione whispers to Harry: 'Look at her eyes. They've been fighting again. Her and Dean.' Harry then stands as she reaches the table - 'the only one' - framed as romantic gallantry.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is one of the most damaging substitutions in the corpus. The book's Ginny earns her place at Slughorn's table through a display of impressive, independent magical ability. The film replaces this with romantic distress over a boyfriend argument, making her flustered and emotionally reactive - the opposite of her book characterisation. Her presence at the supper is now explained by a relationship problem rather than her own formidable skill. This fundamentally alters how the audience understands her competence and agency.

damaging_scenes.scene: HBP Film Corpus Scene 16 (Burrow Christmas - tart-feeding scene)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, the Christmas scenes at the Burrow feature Ginny as one of several family members present. Her interactions with Harry at Christmas are warm but not specially intimate - she is part of group scenes. The romantic tension simmers through Harry's internal narration rather than through choreographed intimate gestures.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film invents a scene where Ginny approaches Harry during the adult conversation, says 'Open up, you' and pops a small tart into his mouth. She smiles at him and hooks her hair over one ear. Harry is visibly affected. Ron immediately plops down between them.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The invented tart-feeding moment constructs their relationship around cute romantic gestures rather than the mutual respect and shared history the book builds. It also makes Ginny the romantic initiator in a slightly coy, food-as-flirtation register that is alien to her book characterisation. Small but contributes to a cumulative pattern of misrepresenting the nature of their dynamic.

damaging_scenes.scene: HBP Film Corpus Scene 17 (Burrow second floor - Ginny in robe, wet hair)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: There is no equivalent scene in the book corpus. The book does not feature a private nighttime encounter between Harry and Ginny at the Burrow where they are alone together in an intimate atmosphere before the Death Eater attack.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film creates an entirely invented scene where Harry finds Ginny alone on the second floor, in a robe, twisting her wet hair in a towel. She tells him 'I don't sleep these days. So I wash my hair.' There is a charged silence, a 'knowing' look from Ginny, and she says 'Happy Christmas, Harry' before the attack begins.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This invented scene is the film's primary vehicle for establishing romantic connection between Harry and Ginny, but it does so through a conventionally 'pretty girl alone at night' staging that is entirely disconnected from how the book builds their relationship - through Quidditch, sibling-group banter, shared courage, and Harry's gradual internal recognition. The scene renders Ginny as a romantic object in a soft-lit intimate setting rather than as the confident, active person the book establishes.

damaging_scenes.scene: HBP Film Corpus Scenes 19-20 (Burrow attack in the reeds - Ginny fights alongside Harry)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The Death Eater attack on the Burrow at Christmas does not occur in the books at all. It is a wholly invented film scene.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film creates an extended action sequence where Harry and Ginny pursue Bellatrix and Greyback through burning reeds, fight side by side, and together blast Greyback with simultaneous jinxes. Ginny warns Harry of the trap and they face the enemy as a pair.
damaging_scenes.explanation: While this invented scene gives Ginny some action agency, it manufactures a bond between Harry and Ginny through shared danger rather than through the organic relationship-building of the books. It also removes the domestic, character-rich Burrow scenes that the book uses to develop Ginny's personality. The scene contributes to the film's pattern of replacing character depth with romantic-action spectacle. The impact weight is moderated because Ginny is at least shown as courageous and capable here.

damaging_scenes.scene: HBP Film Corpus Scene 21 (Corridor - Ginny glimpsed sitting with Dean)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, the scene of Ginny sitting with Dean in Madam Puddifoot's and Harry's jealous thoughts about it is rendered through Harry's internal narration with considerable texture - 'his thoughts strayed to Ginny,' she and Dean were 'cozily closeted,' and Harry scowls. The complexity of his feelings is fully rendered.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film shows Ginny in an alcove 'sitting by as Dean laughs with Seamus,' giving a 'feeble wave' to Harry. She appears peripheral and slightly detached from Dean even here.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Minor loss, but the film consistently drains Ginny and Dean's relationship of credibility, making Ginny look only half-engaged with him, which shortchanges the book's authentic depiction of her having a real relationship before Harry.

damaging_scenes.scene: HBP Film Corpus Scenes 23-25 (Room of Requirement - Ginny hides the book and kisses Harry)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Harry and Ginny's first kiss happens spontaneously in the Gryffindor common room after Gryffindor wins the Quidditch Cup. Harry catches the Snitch, Ginny throws her arms around him with 'a hard, blazing look,' and 'without thinking, without planning it, without worrying about the fact that fifty people were watching, Harry kissed her.' The kiss is impulsive, public, triumphant, and entirely Harry's action. It follows many chapters of slow-burn tension. Ginny's 'hard blazing look' is a recurring motif of her strength.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film entirely replaces the book's kiss with an invented scene in the Room of Requirement. Ginny orchestrates everything: she leads Harry there, takes his book, tells him to close his eyes, then kisses him herself as 'another secret of sorts. One of mine.' She initiates, controls the staging, and frames it as a secret. Harry is passive - he simply stands with his eyes closed and receives the kiss.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is the most structurally damaging change in the corpus. The book's first kiss is one of its most carefully earned moments: a public, joyful, impulsive act by Harry after chapters of internal conflict, enabled by his hard-won courage and Ginny's complete self-possession. The film transfers all agency to Ginny in a way that actually reduces the dramatic payoff - it becomes a coy romantic gesture in a private space rather than a public declaration. More critically, the Quidditch Cup context - which is the culmination of Harry's season-long arc of recognising Ginny as his equal on the pitch and as a person - is completely severed. The 'hard, blazing look' that makes the kiss meaningful is absent. The film also loses the public/social dimension: 'without worrying about the fact that fifty people were watching' is a key beat in Harry's character development. The substitution also means the film never has its Quidditch triumph kiss scene, one of the most beloved and structurally significant moments in the novel.

damaging_scenes.scene: HBP Film Corpus Scene 28 (Courtyard - Ginny comforts Harry after Dumbledore's death)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, it is Ginny who leads Harry away from Dumbledore's body - 'a much smaller and warmer hand had enclosed his and was pulling him upward' - identified only by 'a trace of flowery scent.' This is rendered as wordless, instinctive, deeply intimate. She simply knows what he needs without being told. In the hospital wing she delivers hard news plainly and answers his questions directly. The book also describes Harry looking away from Ginny at the funeral so she won't see his tears.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film has Hermione 'give Ginny a nudge' before she steps forward to comfort Harry. Ginny kneels beside him and he puts his head on her shoulder as she strokes him. The action is prompted by Hermione rather than being Ginny's own instinctive response.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's version is one of the most powerful demonstrations of Ginny's emotional intelligence and her unique connection to Harry - she acts alone, on instinct, guided by her understanding of him. The film's version requires Hermione to initiate the gesture, reducing Ginny's action from a spontaneous expression of deep connection to a prompted response. This is a meaningful loss in a key emotional scene.

damaging_scenes.scene: HBP Film Corpus Scene 30 (Astronomy Tower - final scene, Hermione tells Harry Ron is 'okay with' him and Ginny)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, the ending contains Harry's decision to break up with Ginny at Dumbledore's funeral, a full and moving scene where Ginny accepts it with dignity: 'I knew you wouldn't be happy unless you were hunting Voldemort. Maybe that's why I like you so much.' She does not cry. Harry walks away alone. The breakup is a full scene of emotional maturity on both their parts. Ron gives 'a tiny jerk of the head' signaling acceptance of Harry and Ginny's relationship only at the moment of the kiss.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film ends with Hermione telling Harry that Ron is 'okay with it, you know. You and Ginny. But if I were you, when he's around, I'd keep the snogging to a minimum.' There is no breakup scene. Ginny stands silently with Ron in the background as Harry and Hermione discuss the Horcruxes. The film ends with the four of them at the ramparts. Ginny has no final dialogue of significance and no agency in the ending of her relationship arc.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's ending with Ginny is one of her finest moments: she accepts Harry's decision without self-pity, articulates why she loves him in a way that reveals both her own depth and her understanding of Harry. 'I knew you wouldn't be happy unless you were hunting Voldemort' is a line that encapsulates her maturity, her insight into Harry, and her own strength. The film eliminates this entirely. Ginny ends the film as a silent background presence while Harry and Hermione carry the emotional and thematic weight of the final scene. Her arc - from girl with a crush, to confident young woman, to Harry's equal in a real relationship - has no resolution. This is a significant arc-level loss.

damaging_scenes.scene: HBP Film Corpus - absence of Ron/Ginny corridor confrontation scene
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book contains an extended, dramatically important scene where Ron catches Ginny and Dean kissing in a corridor, leading to a fierce argument in which Ginny tears into Ron about his hypocrisy and double standards, draws her wand, fires a hex at him, and delivers: 'Harry's snogged Cho Chang! And Hermione snogged Viktor Krum, it's only you who acts like it's something disgusting, Ron, and that's because you've got about as much experience as a twelve-year-old!' This scene shows Ginny's fierce independence, her willingness to fight for her autonomy, her sharp tongue, and her loyalty to her own choices. It is one of the defining Ginny scenes in the novel.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: This scene does not appear in the film corpus at all. The film has no equivalent confrontation between Ginny and Ron about her relationships.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The absence of this scene is one of the most damaging omissions. It is the fullest expression of Ginny's voice, her independence, her willingness to challenge authority (even family authority), and her sharp awareness of double standards. The book's Ginny is someone who fights back when her autonomy is threatened. The film never shows this dimension of her at all, replacing it with a Ginny who is primarily defined by her romantic relationship with Harry. The scene also contains crucial context for understanding her relationship history and why Harry falls for her.

damaging_scenes.scene: HBP Film Corpus - absence of Ginny/Ron argument aftermath and Harry's extended internal conflict
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Following the corridor incident, the book devotes several chapters to Harry's internal struggle: 'It's just because she's Ron's sister... She's Ron's sister. She's out-of-bounds.' He lies awake trying to suppress feelings, notices Ginny at practice and deliberately avoids her, finds himself 'laughing with her, walking back from practice with her,' plans around Felix Felicis, and has a 'monster in his chest' metaphor running throughout. This extended internal arc is fundamental to Harry's characterisation and the romance's emotional weight.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film has essentially no equivalent of Harry's extended internal conflict about Ginny. His feelings are established through Hermione's external observation ('I know, Harry. You're my best friend. I see how you look at her') and a dormitory conversation with Ron about her 'nice skin.' There is no 'monster in his chest,' no sleepless nights, no suppressed jealousy at Quidditch practice.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's romance between Harry and Ginny works because we live inside Harry's slowly awakening feelings in granular detail. The film externalises this to Hermione's observations and Ron's dormitory chat. This does not damage Ginny directly, but it means the audience has no emotional investment in their relationship as it has been built - which in turn makes Ginny's role as Harry's romantic partner feel structurally thin. The damage to the adaptation of Ginny is that half the relationship's emotional architecture is simply absent.

damaging_scenes.scene: HBP Film Corpus - absence of Ginny defending Harry against Hermione after Sectumsempra
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, after Harry uses Sectumsempra on Draco and is given detention, Ginny snaps at Hermione: 'Give it a rest, Hermione! By the sound of it, Malfoy was trying to use an Unforgivable Curse, you should be glad Harry had something good up his sleeve!' And when Hermione presses on: 'Oh, don't start acting as though you understand Quidditch, you'll only embarrass yourself.' This leaves Harry 'unbelievably cheerful all of a sudden' despite everything. It shows Ginny's loyalty, her directness, and her willingness to challenge Hermione.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: This exchange does not appear in the film corpus. The film has the Sectumsempra aftermath but no Ginny-Hermione confrontation in the common room.
damaging_scenes.explanation: A small but telling loss. The scene shows Ginny operating as a fully independent presence in the trio's dynamic, not merely as Harry's girlfriend. Her willingness to challenge Hermione - who is intimidating to most characters - is characteristic of her self-assurance. Its absence leaves Ginny with no scene in the film where she actively defends Harry out of her own conviction.

damaging_scenes.scene: HBP Film Corpus - absence of Ginny's Quidditch characterisation (Ron-punching scene, life-of-team at practice)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book depicts Ginny as the 'life and soul of the team' at practice after her Dean breakup, doing imitations of Ron and Harry that keep everyone amused. She calls Ron a 'prat' after he punches Demelza, and Harry has to remind her she's 'not the Captain of this team' while suppressing a laugh. She scores four goals in the match against Slytherin. She is a fully realised Quidditch player with a strong presence in team dynamics.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film shows Ginny flying well in the tryouts montage and making a goal in the Quidditch match, but the richer team-dynamic scenes - her imitations, her calling Ron a prat, Harry's internal reaction to her humor - are absent. Her Quidditch presence is visual but not characterful.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book uses Quidditch practice as one of the primary settings for establishing Ginny's personality: her humor, her leadership instinct, her ease in male spaces, and her specific effect on Harry. The film uses it only to show she can fly. The result is that a major dimension of why Harry falls for her - her funny, confident, totally-at-home presence in his sporting world - is never conveyed.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 5 (INT. KITCHEN - MORNING) — the zip-up/birthday kiss scene
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book scenes 70–93 establish Harry's birthday meeting with Ginny in her room as a tightly controlled, emotionally layered moment. Ginny is composed and rarely weepy; she takes the initiative with wit ('There's the silver lining I've been looking for'), kisses Harry with intensity, and afterward maintains dignified restraint when Ron interrupts — turning away to hide tears but not collapsing. The scene is built on private intimacy, Ginny's self-possession, and Harry's internal conflict about ending the relationship for her safety.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film replaces this with a dress zip-up scene in the kitchen on the morning of the wedding. Ginny is passive — she presents her back and Harry lingers over her skin. The kiss that follows is initiated by physical proximity and lingering touch rather than Ginny's deliberate, witty agency. The scene is framed as romantic-sensual staging rather than an emotionally complex farewell, and George's comic interruption deflates it into a gag. Ginny's voice ('So then I thought, I'd like you to have something to remember me by') and her rare show of vulnerability are entirely absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's birthday scene is the primary establishment of book-Ginny's character in DH: her wit, emotional toughness, deliberate agency, and the bittersweet stakes of the relationship. Replacing it with a passive, physically coded moment strips Ginny of her defining voice and reduces her romantic role to a decorative one. The loss of her wry dialogue and self-composed grief also removes the audience's best opportunity in this film to understand who she is independently of Harry.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 5 — absence of the book's private conversation about Voldemort/the mission
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book scenes 45–50 show Ginny in a private moment with Harry laying the table, shrewdly reading her mother's strategy, and then reacting with whitening face when Harry accidentally reveals he is hunting Voldemort. She asks 'So it's true? That's what you're trying to do?' — demonstrating perceptiveness, courage, and emotional stakes in Harry's mission that are personal to her.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film scene has Ginny ask only whether Harry will tell Ron and Hermione about the mission, framing her concern narrowly. The exchange about Voldemort and her visceral, frightened reaction ('her face whiten') is absent. Her sharp perception of her mother's delaying tactics is also gone.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book beat shows Ginny as perceptive and emotionally invested in Harry's quest in a way that goes beyond romantic attachment. Losing it flattens her into a girlfriend waiting to be kissed rather than someone who grasps the mortal stakes and responds with courage.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 3 (EXT. THE BURROW - NIGHT) — arrival after the Seven Potters
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book scenes 7–18 show Ginny actively informing Harry about the missing portkeys (pointing at each one, tracking arrivals, checking her watch), shouting 'Mum!' to alert the group to George's arrival, and later taking Harry's hand in the dark yard as fear envelops him. She is the emotional anchor and practical information source in this sequence, and the hand-holding is a quiet but significant act of solidarity.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film compresses Ginny to a frightened bystander who shakes her head when Harry asks if anyone is back and delivers one line ('Ron and Tonks should've already been back. Dad and Fred as well.'). The hand-holding in the yard, her systematic tracking of portkeys, and her role as Harry's quiet support during the vigil are all absent. Her reaction to George ('Oh my God! George!') replaces the book's more distributed, active role with a single emotional outburst.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book uses this sequence to show Ginny as competent, calm under pressure, and emotionally attuned to Harry. The film reduces her to a reactive bystander. The lost hand-holding moment is particularly damaging because it is one of the few physical expressions of the relationship's depth in DH's early section, and it occurs at a moment of real fear — establishing Ginny as Harry's source of grounding, not just a romantic backdrop.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 3/4 — absence of Ginny tending to George
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book scenes 11–13 show Ginny gasping at George's wound, helping carry him in, and then tending to him alongside Mrs. Weasley while Harry watches — she is actively present and useful in a moment of family crisis.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film gives Ginny one alarmed exclamation ('Oh my God! George!') and does not show her tending to him. The camera moves away from her. Her role as a capable, caring family member in crisis is not established.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Minor but cumulative: the book repeatedly shows Ginny as practically capable and emotionally resilient in family crises. Each film omission of such moments erodes the overall impression of her competence.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 6 (INT./EXT. MARQUEE) — wedding reception
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book scenes 99–111 show Ginny at the wedding with layered detail: she clears her throat loudly at Gabrielle's flirtatious attention to Harry (showing humor and possessiveness), winks at Harry when Muriel criticises her dress (showing irreverence and confidence), and Harry watches her dancing while restraining himself per his promise to Ron — establishing ongoing romantic tension and her vivid presence.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film shows Ginny laughing as Fred and George rush the dance floor but gives her no lines and no individual characterization at the wedding. The wink, the throat-clear, and the charged look across the dance floor are absent. She appears briefly in the chaos of the Death Eater attack — drawing her wand with 'copper hair gleaming, eyes flashing' — but this is a visual beat, not characterization.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The wedding is one of Ginny's last scenes before the long absence of the hunt. The book uses it to cement her humor, confidence, and the ongoing romantic tension. The film renders her decorative. The visual flourish of her drawing her wand in the chaos is actually somewhat faithful to the book's note about her blazing look, but the preceding characterization that makes it meaningful is absent.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 7 (EXT. LONDON STREET) — Hermione mentions the birthday cake
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: There is no book equivalent of Hermione mentioning a birthday cake that she and Ginny had prepared. The book's birthday scene is in Ginny's room (book scenes 70–93). The cake in the book is the Snitch-shaped one Mrs. Weasley brings out at the garden party (book scene 100).
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Hermione tells Harry that 'Ginny and I had prepared a cake' for his birthday at the wedding. This retroactively replaces the private birthday scene in Ginny's room with an off-screen domestic gesture, further diminishing the significance of Ginny's individual relationship with Harry.
damaging_scenes.explanation: By replacing the intimate, agentive birthday scene with a passing reference to a cake, the film signals to the audience that Ginny's role in Harry's birthday was one of collective domestic support rather than a charged, private romantic farewell. It compounds the damage from the replaced zip-up scene by closing off even the implicit reference to what was lost.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 8 (INT. HOGWARTS EXPRESS) — Ginny's brief appearance on the train
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book scene 120 has Harry imagining Ginny, Neville, and Luna sitting together on the train, 'perhaps wondering where he, Ron, and Hermione were, or debating how best to undermine Snape's new regime' — framing her as active and resistive even in absence. Book scene 143 confirms she was banned from Hogsmeade and had been continuing Dumbledore's Army.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film shows Ginny seated passively in a compartment with other students as Dark Wizards move through the train. She has no lines and no agency. Neville bars the searchers' way and speaks defiantly; Ginny is simply present.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The one film moment establishing what Ginny is doing while Harry is away on the hunt reduces her to a passenger. Her role as a DA leader and resistance organiser at Hogwarts — one of her most significant characterisation points in the book — is not established here and receives no other scene in the film corpus. This is structural absence damage.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 11 (INT. ROOM OF REQUIREMENT) — Ginny's return to Hogwarts
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book scene 169 describes Harry's complex reaction to Ginny climbing through the wall: 'His heart seemed to fall... he had never been less pleased to see her' alongside 'he had forgotten, he had never fully appreciated, how beautiful she was.' She gives him a 'radiant smile.' This captures Harry's love for her in direct conflict with his fear for her safety — one of the most emotionally rich moments of their relationship in DH. Book scene 175 then shows Ginny asserting herself by redirecting Cho away from Harry ('No, Luna will take Harry'), a small but telling act of territorial confidence.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Ginny enters, says 'Harry' and Harry says 'Hey there.' Ron notes that she hasn't seen him in six months and is ignoring her own brother. Ginny then delivers plot-necessary exposition ('Snape knows. He knows Harry was spotted in Hogsmeade.'). The emotional complexity of Harry's reaction — the conflict between love and fear — is entirely absent, and Ginny's redirect of Cho does not appear in the film corpus.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is the reunion scene after months apart under life-threatening conditions. The book invests it with layered emotional conflict that defines Harry's love for Ginny as something he carries painfully. The film makes it a brief greeting and plot delivery. The loss of the Cho redirection also removes a moment of Ginny's quiet, confident assertion within the relationship.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 12 (INT. MARBLE STAIRCASE) — Harry takes Ginny's hand
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: No direct equivalent in the book corpus for this specific staircase hand-hold. The closest book parallel is the hand-holding in the dark yard (book scene 23) and the brief held look during the battle (book scenes 169, 185). The book's Ginny does not passively receive Harry's touch in a crowd — she acts independently.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Harry 'enfolds Ginny's hand in his own' from behind as they walk in a crowd; 'she doesn't look back, knows it's him, knows his touch.' She is entirely passive and receptive.
damaging_scenes.explanation: While romantic, this moment consistently frames Ginny as the passive recipient of Harry's gestures rather than an equal agent in their relationship. Cumulatively, this pattern — zip-up, hand-hold initiated by Harry — reverses the book's dynamic where Ginny frequently acts first (taking his hand in the yard, kissing him on his birthday, redirecting Cho).

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 13 (INT. GREAT HALL) — Ginny steps in front of Harry when Pansy points him out
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: No exact equivalent scene in the book corpus for this specific beat. The book does not have a Great Hall confrontation of this kind in DH.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: When Pansy Parkinson shouts to grab Harry, 'Ginny steps in front of Harry, wand drawn.' This is a protective gesture but framed as instinctive and immediately superseded by the collective Gryffindor line forming around Harry.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is one of the few moments in the film where Ginny shows independent courage and acts first. However, it is a small, immediately absorbed beat. It is scored here only to note that while it is a positive characterisation moment, it is not from the book corpus and does not compensate for the broader pattern of passive portrayal established elsewhere. Net damage from this scene alone is low; it is not an unfaithful scene but a film-original addition.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 17/18 (EXT. WOODEN BRIDGE) — Ginny on the bridge with Neville and Seamus
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book corpus does not contain a detailed bridge-destruction sequence. However, the book establishes Ginny as a DA leader who actively organized resistance at Hogwarts (book scene 143) and fought alongside Harry in the final battle (book scenes 206, 236). Her role in the battle should reflect command and initiative.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Ginny stands at the far end of the bridge, raises her wand 'ready to detonate the spells' but never fires — Neville detonates them instead. She then hoists Neville up, shakes her head at the 'mad' boys, and says 'Mad. The both of you.' Her role is observer, steadier, and commentator rather than combatant.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is one of the film's primary action sequences featuring Ginny, and she does not fire her wand. The detonation — the functional act — belongs to Neville, then Seamus. Ginny's line ('Mad. The both of you.') codes her as the sensible bystander rather than a co-combatant. Book Ginny's battle role — sending 'well-aimed jinx[es] into a crowd of fighters below' (book scene 206) and duelling Bellatrix alongside Hermione and Luna (book scene 236) — is defined by active, skilled combat. Starting her battle portrayal with an un-fired wand undermines this.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 19 (INT. MARBLE STAIRCASE) — 'I know' moment
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book scene 185 shows Ginny looking at Harry 'beseechingly' when Mrs. Weasley orders her to leave the battle, and Harry shakes his head. She turns away 'bitterly.' The book's last extended exchange between them in the battle is characterized by painful, wordless communication and Ginny's thwarted desire to fight alongside him.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Harry says 'Ginny! Neville! You alright?' Neville responds at length about Luna. Harry and Ginny then turn to each other: 'Their eyes catch. An instant, a moment of meaning in the midst of madness.' Ginny says 'I know.' Then she runs off. This is a compressed, stylized farewell.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The film reduces the final in-battle exchange between Harry and Ginny to a single oblique 'I know' — atmospheric but empty of the specific emotional content of the book. The book's version is about her bitterness at being excluded from fighting beside him, and Harry's helpless conflict between love and protection. 'I know' carries none of that weight and leaves the relationship's final battle beat as mood rather than meaning.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 21 (EXT. HOGWARTS GROUNDS) — Ginny with the injured girl
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book scenes 221–228 show Harry passing Ginny in the invisibility cloak as she comforts a girl whispering for her mother. Ginny's voice 'broke' as she says 'I know.' Harry desperately wants to be stopped, to call out to her, but forces himself on. This is one of the most emotionally devastating passages in the book — Harry's love for Ginny as the last thing tethering him to the living world before his death walk.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film reproduces this scene with reasonable fidelity: Ginny says 'It's all right. We're going to get you inside' and 'Don't worry. I won't leave you. I promise.' Ginny's face is 'haunted by sorrow.' Harry watches, 'moved,' then continues. Ginny turns and finds 'only darkness.' The book's 'her voice broke' equivalent is present in spirit. However, Harry's internal monologue — wanting to shout, wanting to be stopped, the visceral pull of her as a reason to live — is necessarily absent in film and not conveyed through cinematography described in the corpus.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The scene itself is among the more faithful in the film corpus, but without access to Harry's interior — his desperate longing to call out to her, his recognition of her as the embodiment of the life he is surrendering — the scene becomes a poignant vignette of Ginny's compassion rather than the agonizing capstone of Harry and Ginny's relationship. The damage is real but inherent to the medium shift; it is scored lower accordingly.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 23 (EXT. COURTYARD) — Ginny's reaction to Harry's apparent death
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book scene 235 has Ron's, Hermione's, and Ginny's voices calling 'Harry!
