HARRY!' when Hagrid carries his body — described as 'worse than McGonagall's' to Harry, who has to make himself lie still. Book scene 234 names all three. The voices are a chorus of unbearable loss, and Ginny's is one of the three that most tempts Harry to break.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Ginny shouts 'No... NO!' and rushes toward Voldemort, but Arthur physically restrains her. Voldemort calls her 'Stupid girl.' Arthur 'wraps his daughter in his arms, letting her struggle briefly before pulling her tighter, closer, safer.' Ginny then becomes absorbed into the family group and has no further individual moment.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The film's staging physically contains Ginny — she rushes forward but is immediately captured by Arthur and held. While dramatically effective, this removes her individual voice (the 'Harry! HARRY!' cry that torments the lying-still Harry in the book) and replaces it with a physical struggle that is immediately suppressed. Her grief is rendered as wild and immediately contained rather than as a devastating personal cry that nearly breaks Harry's resolve. Voldemort's 'stupid girl' dismissal then frames her grief as foolish rather than as the most human and meaningful response in the scene.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film — structural absence of Ginny's Hogwarts resistance arc
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book scenes 133–137 and 143 establish that Ginny tried to steal the Sword of Gryffindor, was punished by being sent to the Forbidden Forest, had been banned from Hogsmeade, and was one of the core leaders of Dumbledore's Army's resistance under Snape and the Carrows. Book scene 163 (Neville) confirms 'Ginny never came back after Easter' — she was removed from Hogwarts for her resistance activity. This is a complete arc of courage and leadership running parallel to Harry's hunt.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film corpus contains no scene depicting or referencing Ginny's resistance activities at Hogwarts — the sword theft attempt, the DA leadership, the punishment, or her removal from school. Her arrival in the Room of Requirement (Film Scene 11) is her first appearance at Hogwarts in the film; no context is given for what she has been doing or what it cost her.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is the most damaging single absence in the film corpus. Ginny's Hogwarts resistance arc is her primary independent narrative in DH — the thing she does that is entirely hers, not contingent on Harry's presence. It establishes her as a leader, establishes her courage as costly (she is expelled mid-year), and gives her arrival at the final battle the weight of someone who has already been fighting. Without it, she arrives in the Room of Requirement as a plot-convenient love interest rather than as a warrior who has been holding the front. Her battle conduct consequently reads as reactive rather than as the continuation of months of resistance.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film — structural absence of Harry watching Ginny's dot on the Marauder's Map
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book scenes 141 and 148 show Harry repeatedly taking out the Marauder's Map not to track Ron (who doesn't appear) but to watch Ginny's dot in the girls' dormitory — 'wondering whether the intensity with which he gazed at it might break into her sleep, that she would somehow know he was thinking about her.' This establishes the depth and ache of Harry's feelings for Ginny during the long dark months of the hunt.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film has no equivalent moment. Ron mentions listening to the radio 'to make sure I don't hear Ginny's name or Fred or George or Mum' — but this is Ron's line, not Harry's. Harry's private, obsessive tenderness toward Ginny during the hunt is not depicted.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The Marauder's Map moments are the primary evidence in the book that Harry's feelings for Ginny are not merely romantic but constitute a deep, sustaining attachment that he carries through the hunt's worst periods. Without them, the film's Harry has no visible interior life in relation to Ginny during the hunt, making their reunion moments feel unmotivated rather than the culmination of months of silent longing.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 24 (INT. GREAT HALL - DAWN) — aftermath, Bellatrix duel
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book scene 236 shows Ginny duelling Bellatrix alongside Hermione and Luna — 'all battling their hardest, but Bellatrix was equal to them' — and a Killing Curse nearly hitting Ginny, provoking Mrs. Weasley's intervention. Ginny is one of three named combatants who together challenge Bellatrix before Mrs. Weasley takes over.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: A bolt 'just misses Ginny' and Mrs. Weasley shouts 'NOT MY DAUGHTER, YOU BITCH!' The film does not show Ginny duelling Bellatrix. She is a near-miss victim, not a combatant. The three-on-one duel that precedes Mrs. Weasley's intervention is absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Reducing Ginny from an active duelist to a passive near-miss victim in the Bellatrix sequence is a significant agency loss. In the book, she is fighting — 'battling her hardest' — which is what provokes Voldemort's near-fatal curse and Mrs. Weasley's protective rage. In the film, she is simply almost hit, which makes Mrs. Weasley's line feel protective of a bystander rather than of a fighter. The 'NOT MY DAUGHTER' line loses half its resonance when the daughter was not herself in combat.
